explanations.explanation: That's the pair, baker. God says, "You must not follow the practices of the land of Egypt, where you used to live, and you must not follow the practices of the land of Canaan, into which I am bringing you." (Leviticus 18:3) One land is behind them and one is ahead of them, and neither one is the pattern. Two lands, one answer.

Half right, friend, and Canaan is the half that counts. The text says the other land is Egypt, "…where you used to live…" (Leviticus 18:3) Babylon never shows up in this passage. Egypt was Israel's old address, and Canaan was the new one God was bringing them into.

Egypt is the right one, baker! The second land is Canaan, though, not Assyria. God says it is the land "…into which I am bringing you." (Leviticus 18:3) Assyria never comes up here. God is talking about the place Israel left and the place Israel is headed.

Nope, baker, no building your own recipe in the middle. God says, "You are to practice My judgments and keep My statutes by walking in them." (Leviticus 18:4) The way is His, not a compromise between two other ways. Then He signs it again: "I am the LORD your God."

False is right, friend. God doesn't say, "Go find a middle road." He says, "You are to practice My judgments and keep My statutes by walking in them. I am the LORD your God." (Leviticus 18:4) Israel's way is God's way, start to finish. Nobody has to invent anything.

explanations.answer: The man who does them will live by them
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. God says, "Keep My statutes and My judgments, for the man who does these things will live by them. I am the LORD." (Leviticus 18:5) The reason isn't applause or scared enemies. It's life. And He puts His name on it at the end.

explanations.answer: The nations around them will honor them
explanations.explanation: I get why that sounds nice, friend, but God never says it here. His reason is, "…the man who does these things will live by them." (Leviticus 18:5) The nations clapping isn't on the list. The reason is living by them.

explanations.answer: Their enemies will run away from them
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Nobody's running anywhere in this verse, and I'm the one who spent years in a drawer, so trust me, I know about running nowhere. God's reason is, "…the man who does these things will live by them." (Leviticus 18:5) That's a promise about life, not a battle plan.

Nations, baker, that's the one. God says, "…by all these things the nations I am driving out before you have defiled themselves." (Leviticus 18:24) So He's pointing to the nations already in the land. He's the One driving them out, too.

Priests would be a fun guess, friend, but it's not in this verse. God says it was "…the nations I am driving out before you…" that defiled themselves. (Leviticus 18:24) Nobody here is pointing at priests. The nations are the ones He's driving out.

Kings sound like a big word, baker, but that's not what God says. The verse says, "…the nations I am driving out before you have defiled themselves." (Leviticus 18:24) It's whole nations, not a few rulers. Good try, though.

Yep, and it's a blunt one, baker. God says, "Even the land has become defiled, so I am punishing it for its sin, and the land will vomit out its inhabitants." (Leviticus 18:25) I think this is a heavy picture. The land itself is part of this, and it is the land that does the vomiting out.
Swallowing is the opposite direction, friend! God says the land "…will vomit out its inhabitants." (Leviticus 18:25) Out, not in. I think that picture sticks in your head on purpose.

Hiding sounds gentler, baker, but that's not the verse. God says the land "…will vomit out its inhabitants." (Leviticus 18:25) The land pushes them out, and nothing here says it hides anybody. It's a strong picture.

True, baker. God says, "…you must not commit any of these abominations—neither your native-born nor the foreigner who lives among you." (Leviticus 18:26) The native-born and the foreigner living among them are both named. Nobody gets a different rulebook.
Not false, friend. God names the foreigner outright: "…neither your native-born nor the foreigner who lives among you." (Leviticus 18:26) The text says it covers both. Nobody gets skipped.

Not quite, baker. God says the opposite: "So if you defile the land, it will vomit you out as it spewed out the nations before you." (Leviticus 18:28) Being brought into the land doesn't mean anything goes there. God spells out the "if," and the same thing that happened to the nations could happen to Israel.

False is right, baker. God says, "So if you defile the land, it will vomit you out as it spewed out the nations before you." (Leviticus 18:28) Getting in the door doesn't mean you can do anything inside. The same thing that happened to them could happen to Israel.

explanations.answer: He must be cut off from his people
explanations.explanation: That's what God says, baker. "Therefore anyone who commits any of these abominations must be cut off from among his people." (Leviticus 18:29) It's a serious line, and I think it's meant to be. He means it for anyone, no exceptions named.

explanations.answer: He must offer a lamb at the altar
explanations.explanation: A lamb is a good guess, friend, but this verse doesn't mention one. God says such a person "…must be cut off from among his people." (Leviticus 18:29) No altar and no lamb show up here. It's a heavy verse, so I'll keep it straight.

explanations.answer: He must stay outside the camp a week
explanations.explanation: A week outside the camp is a neat idea, baker, but the text doesn't say it. God says the person "…must be cut off from among his people." (Leviticus 18:29) There's no number of days in this verse. The verse is plain and it's a serious one.
